extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in algebraic topology (readers of a standard algebraic topology textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, algebraic properties, and principal theorems about (singular and simplicial) cohomology: dualization of chain complexes, cup/cap products, Universal Coefficient Theorem, Poincaré and Alexander duality, and related constructions. Geared to computing and understanding cohomology groups and their extra structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology is a contravariant functor
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology groups H^i(X) satisfy axioms analogous to homology but induced homomorphisms go in the opposite direction (contravariant rather than covariant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contravariance is the source of extra algebraic structure (e.g. cup product and cohomology operations) not present in homology in the same way. It explains why maps X→Y induce maps H^*(Y)→H^*(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of cup product via diagonal map
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural product (cup product) H^i(X) × H^j(X) → H^{i+j}(X) obtained by composing the cross product H^i(X)×H^j(X) → H^{i+j}(X×X) with the map induced by the diagonal Δ: X → X×X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with homology: homology has a cross product Hi(X)×Hj(X)→Hi+j(X×X), but to get back to Hi+j(X) one would need a map X×X→X (rare). Contravariance makes the diagonal X→X×X available to induce the second map in cohomology. The cup product gives H^*(X) a graded ring structure and is subtler than the additive structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product (homology and cohomology)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural cross product Hi(X) × Hj(Y) → Hi+j(X×Y) in homology (and analogously in cohomology) induced at the chain level by mapping pairs of cells to product cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the first half of constructing cup products (take X=Y). For CW complexes the cellular chains induce the cross product. In cohomology one composes the cross product with the map induced by the diagonal to get the cup product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cochains and coboundary (C^n and δ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a space X and abelian group G, C^n(X;G) = Hom(C_n(X), G) (cochains are functions assigning G-values to singular n-simplices). The coboundary δ: C^n → C^{n+1} is the dual (transpose) of the chain boundary ∂ and satisfies δ^2 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit formula: for (n+1)-simplex σ, δϕ(σ) = Σ (-1)^i ϕ(σ|[v0,...,v̂i,...,vn+1]). Cocycles are elements of Ker δ, coboundaries are Im δ, and H^n(X;G)=Ker δ / Im δ. This concretely identifies cochains with arbitrary functions on simplices and δ with the combinatorial signed restriction sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-dimensional interpretations (H^0, H^1, examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: H^0(X;G) equals the group of functions from path-components of X to G (constant on components). H^1 measures obstructions to solving δϕ=ψ (analogue of 'finding potentials' in calculus); for graphs/simplicial complexes H^1 is product/sum of copies of G corresponding to edges outside a maximal tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If X is a tree, H^1(X;G)=0 (solutions to δϕ=ψ always exist). For G=Z_2 on a surface, δψ=0 corresponds to an even number of 1-values on triangle edges and determines curve systems C_ψ; ψ=δϕ corresponds to those curves being level curves separating regions. These geometric pictures give intuition for cocycle vs coboundary and global vs local obstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology as dualization of a chain complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a chain complex ...→C_{n+1}→C_n→C_{n-1}→... of free abelian groups, cohomology is obtained by applying Hom(–,G) to get the cochain complex ...←Hom(C_{n+1},G)←Hom(C_n,G)←..., with coboundary δ = ∂^* the dual map, and taking cohomology Ker δ / Im δ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal linear-algebraic dualization explains why δ increases degree and why the algebraic relationship between homology and cohomology is governed by Hom and Ext functors. The dual map reverses arrows (hence contravariance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Coefficient Theorem (cohomology) — split short exact sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a chain complex C of free abelian groups and coefficient group G there is a split short exact sequence 0 → Ext(H_{n-1}(C), G) → H^n(C;G) → Hom(H_n(C), G) → 0 (Theorem 3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses H^n(C;G) in terms of the integral homology groups H_n(C) and Ext. The sequence splits (noncanonically), and the Ext-term accounts for torsion phenomena (torsion shifts up one degree in cohomology). The theorem is the cohomological analogue of the universal coefficient theorem for homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and computation of Ext(H,G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key properties: Ext(H⊕H',G) ≅ Ext(H,G) ⊕ Ext(H',G); Ext(H,G)=0 if H is free; Ext(Z_n,G) ≅ G/nG. For finitely generated H, Ext(H,Z) is isomorphic to the torsion subgroup of H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties allow computing Ext terms in the Universal Coefficient Theorem; in particular, when homology groups are finitely generated one gets explicit decompositions of cohomology (see Corollary 3.3). Ext(H,G) can be viewed as classes of extensions 0→G→J→H→0 though that interpretation is usually not needed in topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology from finitely generated homology (Corollary 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If H_n and H_{n-1} are finitely generated with torsion subgroups T_n and T_{n-1}, then H^n(C;Z) ≅ (H_n / T_n) ⊕ T_{n-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus for finitely generated homology the cohomology free part comes from the free part of H_n and torsion in cohomology comes from torsion of H_{n-1}. Example calculations earlier in the text illustrate torsion shifting up one dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturality of the Universal Coefficient short exact sequences and induced isos
rubrics_metrics.description: The short exact sequences of the Universal Coefficient Theorem are natural with respect to chain maps: a chain map inducing isomorphism on homology induces isomorphism on cohomology with any coefficients (Corollary 3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The splitting of the short exact sequence is not natural (depends on choice of projections), and in general a natural splitting need not exist. Naturality of the sequences (but not the splitting) follows from the constructions; use five-lemma arguments when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization to modules over a ring / field coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If one replaces abelian groups by modules over a ring R (principal ideal domain), analogous split short exact sequences hold: 0 → Ext_R(H_{n-1}(C), G) → H^n(C;G) → Hom_R(H_n(C), G) → 0. If R is a field (or modules are free), Ext_R terms vanish and H^n ≅ Hom_R(H_n, R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, with field coefficients cohomology is the exact dual of homology: H^n(X;F) ≅ Hom_F(H_n(X;F), F). This simplifies calculations and eliminates torsion issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced cohomology and relationship to unreduced groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced cohomology groups are obtained by dualizing the augmented chain complex; H^n_red(X;G) = H^n(X;G) for n>0 and H^0 differs by quotienting out constant functions (image of augmentation dual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The augmentation map ε: C_0(X)→Z dualizes to ε^*: Hom(Z,G)→C^0(X;G) producing constant functions; reduced cohomology mod out constants. This mirrors reduced homology and clarifies basepoint-dependent statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative cohomology and the long exact sequence of a pair
rubrics_metrics.description: For a pair (X,A) dualizing 0 → C_n(A) → C_n(X) → C_n(X,A) → 0 gives 0 ← C^n(A;G) ← C^n(X;G) ← C^n(X,A;G) ← 0; relative coboundary maps yield relative cohomology H^n(X,A;G) and a long exact sequence ... → H^n(X,A;G) → H^n(X;G) → H^n(A;G) → H^{n+1}(X,A;G) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative cochains are those functions on simplices of X vanishing on simplices in A. The exactness and LES are obtained directly from the short exact sequence of cochain complexes and duality of maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Čech cohomology via nerves and direct limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For spaces with local pathologies, define Čech cohomology ˇH^i(X;G) as the direct limit lim_{U} H^i(N(U);G) over all open covers U, where N(U) is the nerve simplicial complex of U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Čech cohomology agrees with singular cohomology for CW-like spaces but behaves better for non-locally-contractible sets; example: certain 'shrinking spheres' have pathological singular cohomology but reasonable Čech cohomology. Note: inverse-limit (Čech homology) misbehaves because inverse limits need not preserve exactness; Steenrod homology remedies this for homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré duality and fundamental class (manifolds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an R-orientable closed n-manifold M there is a fundamental class [M] ∈ H_n(M;R) (or in H_n(M,∂M;R) for manifolds with boundary), and cap product with [M] yields isomorphisms DM: H^k(M;R) → H_{n-k}(M;R) (and relative versions in presence of boundary) — including Theorem 3.43 for manifolds with boundary decomposed into A and B giving DM: H^k(M,A;R) → H_{n-k}(M,B;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orientability is characterized by coherent choices of local orientations (generators of local homology). Collar neighborhoods and five-lemma arguments are used in boundary cases. Fundamental classes behave naturally with boundary maps, and Poincaré duality underlies many computations and corollaries (e.g., Alexander duality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alexander duality and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is a compact, locally contractible, nonempty proper subspace of S^n, then Hi(S^n − K; Z) ≅ H^{n−i−1}(K; Z). More generally, for compact locally contractible K ⊂ closed orientable n-manifold M, Hi(M, M−K; Z) ≅ H^{n−i}(K; Z) (Theorem 3.44 and Corollary 3.45).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alexander duality follows from Poincaré duality and the LES of the pair. Requires local contractibility; counterexamples (quasi-circle) show the hypothesis is necessary. Corollary implications include vanishing/torsion constraints on cohomology of compact subsets of R^n (Corollary 3.46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology operations and extra algebraic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond cup product there exist cohomology operations (e.g., Steenrod operations) that make H^*(X) into a module over a nontrivial ring; these operations arise from contravariance and richer algebraic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes these operations are deeper than cup products and defers their treatment. They provide additional algebraic invariants of spaces and play significant roles in homotopy-theoretic descriptions of cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cap product and module structure of homology over cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Cap product gives pairings H_k(X;R) × H^ℓ(X;R) → H_{k−ℓ}(X;R) and makes H_*(X;R) into a right module over H^*(X;R); cap products interact with cup products via (α ∩ ϕ) ∩ ψ = α ∩ (ϕ ∪ ψ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cap product is central to duality theorems (Poincaré duality uses cap with a fundamental class). Exercises point out module properties and compatibility with boundary/coboundary maps; formulas are used to check commutativity up to sign in duality diagrams.
